title: Short-Course Antibiotic Therapy for Pediatric Community-Acquired Pneumonia: Evidence, Limitations, and the Need for Improved Diagnosis
content: Background: Short-course antibiotic therapy is increasingly recommended for children with uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), but uncertainty remains about its applicability to bacterial disease and whether antibiotics are needed in routine pediatric outpatient care settings. Methods: We conducted a narrative review of literature published from January 2010 through September 2026. PubMed/MEDLINE, Google Scholar, ClinicalTrials.gov, agency websites, and reference lists were searched. Evidence was synthesized descriptively; no formal risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis was performed. Results: Systematic reviews and randomized trials indicate that three- to six-day courses can achieve outcomes comparable to longer regimens in children, mainly outpatients with mild, uncomplicated CAP. However, many trials relied on clinical diagnosis, rarely established etiology, and excluded children with severe disease or major comorbidities. Inclusion of children without bacterial infection may have contributed to similar outcomes across treatment durations; evidence is insufficient to establish efficacy in confirmed bacterial CAP or higher-risk populations. Shorter courses reduce antibiotic exposure among treated children but do not determine who needs antibiotics. Lung ultrasound offers a radiation-free point-of-care approach to identifying pneumonia, while procalcitonin and rapid viral testing may refine etiological assessment. Yet evidence for combined diagnostic strategies largely concerns accuracy rather than outpatient prescribing outcomes. Conclusions: Short courses are supported for carefully selected children with uncomplicated CAP, but their generalizability is limited. Improving diagnosis and identifying children likely to benefit from antibiotics may reduce unnecessary use beyond what shortening treatment alone can achieve. Prospective outpatient studies should evaluate whether integrated imaging, biomarkers, and microbiological tests improve prescribing and clinical outcomes.
